questions.question: The Standard Model of matter states that protons are not considered to be fundamental particles because:
questions.answer: Particle accelerator collisions show that protons have internal structure (they are made of quarks), so they are not fundamental (C).
options: protons may spontaneously decay into other particles.
protons can be broken apart in particle accelerators.
protons are a member of the Boson family of particles.

questions.question: Students plotted the radiation of stars against their wavelengths. If a star has a surface temperature of 4000 K, what is the maximum wavelength of the radiation emitted by the star?
questions.answer: Wien's law: $\lambda_{\max}=\dfrac{b}{T}=\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{4000}=7.25\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}=725\ \text{nm}$ (D). (Option C is $7.25\times10^{-5}$ m.)

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the observations of two people, one travelling at 99.9% of the speed of light, and one stationary?
questions.answer: Each observer measures time in their own (proper) frame to pass at the normal rate; time dilation is only observed for the other person's clock (A).
options: Both people will observe time to be passing at the normal rate in their frame of reference.
The person travelling at 99.9% of the speed of light will observe their time to be passing slower.
The stationary person will observe their time to be passing slower.
Both people will observe time to be passing slower in their frame of reference.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about AC induction motors is correct?
questions.answer: The rotor must lag the rotating stator field (slip), otherwise there would be no changing flux through the rotor and no induced current or torque. So the field rotates faster than the rotor (C).
options: There is no current produced in induction motors.
Induction motors need slip rings to operate.
The magnetic field rotates faster than the rotor.
The rotor rotates faster than the magnetic field.

questions.question: A muon is an elementary particle similar to the electron, with an electric charge of $-1e$ but with a much greater mass. A muon and an electron are travelling at the same speed. Which row gives the particle with the greater kinetic energy and the particle with the longer de Broglie wavelength?
questions.answer: $K=\tfrac12mv^2$ is larger for the more massive muon. $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv}$ is larger for the less massive electron. (B)
options: Greater kinetic energy: muon; longer de Broglie wavelength: muon
Greater kinetic energy: muon; longer de Broglie wavelength: electron
Greater kinetic energy: electron; longer de Broglie wavelength: muon
Greater kinetic energy: electron; longer de Broglie wavelength: electron

questions.question: In a Physics class, students observe three light sources through a spectroscope. Experiment 1 uses an incandescent lamp. Experiment 2 uses a sodium lamp. Experiment 3 uses an incandescent lamp with the light passed through sodium vapour. Which row identifies what the students would observe in each experiment?
questions.answer: An incandescent lamp gives a continuous spectrum; sodium vapour excited in a lamp gives an emission spectrum (the yellow doublet on a dark background); white light passed through cool sodium vapour gives an absorption spectrum (the same two wavelengths missing as black lines). (A)
options: 1: continuous spectrum of colours; 2: two yellow lines on a dark background; 3: full-colour background with two black lines
1: continuous spectrum of colours; 2: full-colour background with two black lines; 3: two yellow lines on a dark background
1: two yellow lines on a dark background; 2: full spectrum of colours; 3: full-colour background with two black lines
1: full-colour background with two black lines; 2: two yellow lines on a dark background; 3: full spectrum of colours

questions.question: The diagram shows the perigee and apogee of the Moon, two points in the Moon's elliptical orbit around Earth. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.answer: At perigee (closest to Earth) $U=-\frac{GMm}{r}$ is most negative (minimum), and since total energy is constant, $K$ is maximum, so the Moon moves fastest (C). At apogee $U$ is a maximum and $K$ a minimum.
options: At apogee, its gravitational potential energy as well as its kinetic energy are at minimum. It moves at a low velocity.
At apogee, its gravitational potential energy as well as its kinetic energy are at maximum. It moves at a high velocity.
At perigee, its gravitational potential energy is at a minimum and its kinetic energy is at a maximum. It moves at a high velocity.
At perigee, its gravitational potential energy is at a maximum and its kinetic energy is at a minimum. It moves at a low velocity.

questions.question: Two parallel plates separated by a distance $d$ have a potential difference $V$ across them. A particle with charge $Q$ is placed midway between the plates. What is the magnitude of the electrostatic force acting on the particle?
questions.answer: The field between the plates is uniform, $E=\dfrac Vd$, so $F=QE=\dfrac{QV}{d}$ wherever the particle is (C).

questions.question: $^{27}_{12}\text{Mg}$ can decay by beta minus emission to one of two possible excited states of $^{27}_{13}\text{Al}$. Both excited states decay by emission of a gamma photon directly to the ground state. The diagram shows the energy levels and two routes for the beta decay. One route results in the emission of a gamma photon with a higher frequency than the other. What is the kinetic energy of the beta particle emitted in this route?
questions.answer: The higher-frequency photon comes from the higher excited state, at $1.63\times10^{-13}$ J above the Al-27 ground state. The Mg-27 ground state is $4.18\times10^{-13}$ J above the Al-27 ground state, so $K_\beta=4.18\times10^{-13}-1.63\times10^{-13}=2.55\times10^{-13}\ \text{J}$ (C).

questions.question: A short copper rod R is placed on a pair of thick horizontal parallel copper rails. A horizontal magnetic field exists in the direction shown by the dashed arrows. The diagram shows the apparatus viewed from directly above. When switch S is closed, R will tend to:
questions.answer: Using the right-hand rule on the current in R and the horizontal field shown, the force on R is vertical and upwards, so R tends to lift off the rails (A).
options: lift upwards away from the rails.
be pressed downwards onto the rails.

questions.question: A transformer has 1000 windings on the primary coil and 200 windings on the secondary coil. The primary voltage is 240 V with a primary current of 10.0 A. The secondary current is 44.0 A. What is the efficiency and type of this transformer?
questions.answer: $V_s=240\times\dfrac{200}{1000}=48\ \text{V}$, so it is step-down. $P_{in}=240\times10.0=2400$ W and $P_{out}=48\times44.0=2112$ W, so efficiency $=\dfrac{2112}{2400}=88\%$ (D).

questions.question: For a planet orbiting a single star, which factors determine the planet's orbital period?
questions.answer: $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}=\dfrac{GM}{4\pi^2}$, so $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{GM}}$ depends only on the star's mass and the orbital radius (B).
options: mass of planet; mass of star; radius of orbit
mass of star; radius of orbit
speed of planet; radius of orbit
mass of star; mass of planet

questions.question: An investigation aimed to measure the magnetic permeability constant $\mu_0$. Two wires, both of length 70.0 cm, were arranged horizontally one above the other, 0.50 cm apart, with the bottom wire resting on an electronic balance. When a current of 25.5 A flows through both wires, the reading on the electronic balance changes by 0.500 g. What is the value of $\mu_0$ as determined by this investigation (in $\text{N A}^{-2}$)?

In an investigation measuring $\mu_0$ with two parallel current-carrying wires (wire length 70.0 cm, separation 0.50 cm, current 25.5 A, balance change 0.500 g), which measurement has the greatest relative error?
questions.answer: The separation is the smallest quantity (0.50 cm) measured with a ruler whose uncertainty (about $\pm0.1$ cm) is a large fraction of it, so it has the greatest relative error (B).
options: change in the reading of the electronic balance

questions.question: In the diagrams the loops are initially all the same size and the magnetic field $B$ is the same. (S) The loop is rotated $90^\circ$ in 2.0 s. (T) The magnetic field is reduced to zero in 4.0 s. (U) The loop's radius doubles in 2.0 s. (V) The direction of the magnetic field is reversed in 2.0 s. In which situation would the average induced emf around the loop be the greatest?
questions.answer: With initial flux $\Phi=BA$ ($A=\pi r^2$): S: $\Delta\Phi=BA$ in 2.0 s gives $0.5BA$ per s. T: $BA/4.0=0.25BA$. U: area becomes $4A$, $\Delta\Phi=3BA$ in 2.0 s gives $1.5BA$. V: $\Delta\Phi=2BA$ in 2.0 s gives $BA$. $\varepsilon=\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$ is greatest for U (C).

questions.question: Which statement correctly matches Malus' Law?
questions.answer: Malus' law is $I=I_{\max}\cos^2\theta$ for plane-polarised light incident on an analyser, so the transmitted intensity is directly proportional to $\cos^2\theta$ (A). Note: the school's answer key gives B, which is incorrect (it describes an inverse proportion).
options: The intensity of polarised light entering an analyser is directly proportional to the cosine squared of the angle between the polariser and the analyser.
The intensity of polarised light entering an analyser is inversely proportional to the cosine squared of the angle between the polariser and the analyser.
The intensity of non-polarised light entering an analyser is directly proportional to the cosine squared of the angle between the polariser and the analyser.
The intensity of non-polarised light entering an analyser is inversely proportional to the cosine squared of the angle between the polariser and the analyser.

questions.question: A rectangular coil of dimensions 3.0 cm $\times$ 4.0 cm carries a current of 15.0 mA in a uniform magnetic field of 3.0 T. The coil has 20 turns of wire and is free to rotate about the axis shown. If the coil is rotated by $25^\circ$ (from the position where its plane is parallel to the field), what is the torque acting on the coil?
questions.answer: $\tau=nIAB\cos25^\circ$ (angle measured from the plane of the coil being parallel to the field) $=20\times0.0150\times(0.030\times0.040)\times3.0\times\cos25^\circ=9.79\times10^{-4}$ N m. The direction is anticlockwise as shown by the force directions on the coil sides (B).

questions.question: An engineer turns a nut by applying a constant force to a 25.00 cm spanner at different angles and measures the torque. The graph shows torque against $\sin\theta$ for the data collected. What is the magnitude of the force applied to the nut?
questions.answer: $\tau=rF\sin\theta$, so the gradient of the $\tau$ vs $\sin\theta$ graph equals $rF$. Gradient $\approx\dfrac{200-50}{0.59-0.14}\approx333\ \text{N m}$ so $F=\dfrac{333}{0.2500}\approx1333$ N (D).

questions.question: A rugby ball is kicked with an initial velocity of $20.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $40.0^\circ$ to the horizontal ground. Ignore air resistance and treat the ball as a simple projectile. Determine the minimum velocity of the ball in flight.
questions.answer: The horizontal velocity is constant and the vertical velocity is zero at the top of the flight, so the minimum speed is the horizontal component: $v_{\min}=20.0\cos40.0^\circ=15.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.question: A rugby ball is kicked with an initial velocity of $20.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $40.0^\circ$ to the horizontal ground, and just passes over a crossbar whose top is 3.00 m above the ground, at a time $t$ after it is kicked (on its way down). Ignore air resistance. Find $t$.
questions.answer: Vertically: $u_y=20.0\sin40.0^\circ=12.86\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $a=-9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, $s_y=3.00$ m. Using $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$: $3.00=12.86t-4.9t^2$, so $4.9t^2-12.86t+3.00=0$, $t=0.259$ s or $t=2.36$ s. The ball is above the crossbar on its way up at 0.259 s and descending to it at 2.36 s; the ball just passes over the bar on its way down, so $t=2.36$ s.

questions.question: A rugby ball is kicked with an initial velocity of $20.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $40.0^\circ$ to the horizontal ground, from a horizontal distance of 38 m from the posts. The top of the crossbar is 3.00 m above the ground. Ignore air resistance. Determine whether the ball can pass over the crossbar. Show working.
questions.answer: Time to travel 38 m horizontally: $t=\dfrac{38}{20.0\cos40.0^\circ}=2.48$ s. Height then: $y=(20.0\sin40.0^\circ)(2.48)-\tfrac12(9.8)(2.48)^2=31.9-30.1=1.7$ m. Since $1.7\ \text{m}<3.00$ m the ball is below the crossbar, so it cannot pass over it (it would pass over from 36.3 m, the range at which the ball is at 3.00 m on its way down).

questions.question: A GPS satellite is in a circular orbit at a height $h$ above the surface of the Earth, which has mass $M$ and radius $R$. Use $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}$ to show that the angular speed of the satellite is $\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^3}}$.
questions.answer: Gravity provides the centripetal force, with orbital radius $r=R+h$: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $v^2=\dfrac{GM}{r}$. Since $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}=r\omega$: $r^2\omega^2=\dfrac{GM}{r}$, so $\omega^2=\dfrac{GM}{r^3}$ and $\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^3}}$.

questions.question: The angular speed of a satellite in a circular orbit at height $h$ above the Earth's surface is $\omega=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^3}}$. Calculate the orbital period when $h=2.02\times10^7$ m. Use $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\text{kg}^{-2}$, $M_{E}=5.97\times10^{24}$ kg and $R_E=6.37\times10^{6}$ m.

A satellite of mass 1630 kg is in a circular orbit at a height of $2.02\times10^7$ m above the Earth's surface. Calculate its gravitational potential energy in this orbit. Use $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\text{kg}^{-2}$, $M_{E}=5.97\times10^{24}$ kg and $R_E=6.37\times10^{6}$ m.

A GPS satellite is in a circular orbit around the Earth. A different satellite is in a higher circular orbit. Explain how the linear speed of the higher satellite compares with that of the GPS satellite.
questions.answer: Gravity provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$, independent of the satellite's mass. A higher orbit has a larger radius $r$, so $v$ is smaller: the higher satellite travels more slowly than the GPS satellite.

questions.question: A 1300 kg car makes a turn on a circular bend of road at a speed of 80 km/h. The bend is not banked and has a radius of 40 m. What is the magnitude of the centripetal force required for the car to make this turn?

A 1300 kg car travels on a circular bend of road that is banked at $8^\circ$ to the horizontal. The car is travelling at the maximum speed at which it does not slide up the bank, so friction acts down the slope with its maximum value of $1.60\times10^4$ N (16 049 N). Calculate the magnitude of the centripetal force exerted by the road on the car. Support your answer with a diagram that identifies the relevant forces and vector components. Use $g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.
questions.answer: Forces: weight $F_g=mg$ (down), normal force $F_N$ (perpendicular to the road) and friction $F_f$ (down the slope). Vertical balance: $F_N\cos8^\circ=mg+F_f\sin8^\circ$, so $F_N=\dfrac{1300(9.8)+16049\sin8^\circ}{\cos8^\circ}=1.51\times10^4$ N. The horizontal components of $F_N$ and $F_f$ (towards the centre of the bend) provide the centripetal force: $F_c=F_f\cos8^\circ+F_N\sin8^\circ=16049\cos8^\circ+15121\sin8^\circ=1.80\times10^4\ \text{N}$.

questions.question: A small particle of mass 5.0 mg and charge $+2.0\ \mu\text{C}$ is shot at $30^\circ$ and an initial speed of $4.00\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ into a large gravity-free region between two parallel charged plates 2.0 m apart, with a potential difference of 2000 V across them (the top plate is positive). Find the acceleration of the particle within the gravity-free region.
questions.answer: $E=\dfrac Vd$ and $F=qE=\dfrac{qV}{d}$, with $F=ma$: $a=\dfrac{qV}{md}=\dfrac{(2.0\times10^{-6})(2000)}{(5.0\times10^{-6})(2.0)}=4.0\times10^{2}\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ towards the negative plate (perpendicular to the plates).

questions.question: A small particle of mass 5.0 mg and charge $+2.0\ \mu\text{C}$ is shot at $30^\circ$ to the plates with an initial speed of $4.00\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, from the surface of the negative plate, into a large gravity-free region between two parallel plates 2.0 m apart with a potential difference of 2000 V (acceleration $4.0\times10^2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ towards the negative plate). How far along from its launch position will the particle hit the negative plate?
questions.answer: Perpendicular to the plates: $u_y=4.00\sin30^\circ=2.00\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $a=-4.0\times10^2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. The particle returns to the plate when $v_y=-2.00\ \text{m s}^{-1}$: $t=\dfrac{-2.00-2.00}{-400}=0.010$ s. Parallel to the plates: $u_x=4.00\cos30^\circ=3.46\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (constant), so $\Delta x=3.46\times0.010=3.5\times10^{-2}$ m (3.46 cm). Note: the school's diagram shows the particle launched slightly above the plate without giving a height, so launch from the plate is assumed, as in the school's solution.

questions.question: Rutherford's atomic model placed all the positive charge and most of the mass of an atom in the nucleus. It could not account for the existence of isotopes, where atoms of the same element differ in mass. Outline the way in which the discovery of the particle responsible for this variation in mass was made and explain why the discovery came so much later.
questions.answer:
The particle responsible for isotopes is the neutron: a neutral particle with a mass almost equal to that of the proton, so isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

Chadwick (1932) directed alpha particles from a polonium source at a beryllium target. This produced a highly penetrating, neutral radiation that could not be detected directly by a Geiger counter or ionisation chamber. When this radiation was incident on a block of paraffin wax (rich in hydrogen), protons were knocked out and were detected. Applying conservation of energy and momentum to the collisions showed that the radiation had to consist of neutral particles with a mass about equal to that of the proton, not gamma rays, which could not transfer enough momentum. This confirmed the existence of the neutron.

The neutron was discovered so much later than the proton and electron because it has no charge. It does not ionise matter or interact with the electric fields of atoms, so it passes through matter without leaving a track and cannot be detected directly or deflected by electric or magnetic fields; it could only be detected indirectly through its collisions with other particles.

questions.question: Using the example of a proton moving at $500\ \text{km s}^{-1}$, show that its wavelength is too short to detect using present-day technology.
questions.answer: $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv}=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{(1.673\times10^{-27})(500\times10^{3})}=7.9\times10^{-13}\ \text{m}$. This is much smaller than the diameter of an atom (about $10^{-10}$ m) and the spacing in available diffraction gratings and crystals, so no diffraction or interference effects could be observed with present-day technology.

questions.question: Outline the experimental evidence that led to the development of the formula used to calculate the wavelength of de Broglie's matter waves.
questions.answer: de Broglie proposed that particles have a wavelength $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv}$, extending the wave–particle duality shown by light to matter. He was motivated by evidence that light behaves as a particle (the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering, where X-ray photons transferred momentum to electrons), and by the need to explain Bohr's stationary states and quantised angular momentum for electrons.\n\nExperimental evidence for matter waves came from Davisson and Germer, who fired electrons at a nickel crystal and observed a diffraction pattern with intensity maxima at specific angles, which is only possible if the electrons behave as waves. The wavelength calculated from the crystal spacing and the angles matched $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv}$. Electrons passed through a double slit also produced an interference pattern like that of light, with measurements agreeing with de Broglie's formula. These results show that the wavelength of a particle is Planck's constant divided by its momentum.

questions.question: A technique used to turn pure silicon-28 into a type of material used in semiconductors is to bombard the pure silicon-28 with neutrons from a nuclear reactor. Using appropriate equations, show how the capture of a neutron by a silicon-28 nucleus can result in the transmutation of silicon nuclei into phosphorus by beta decay.
questions.answer:
Neutron capture: $^{28}_{14}\text{Si}+{}^{1}_{0}n\rightarrow{}^{29}_{14}\text{Si}$.

Beta-minus decay of the silicon-29 (a neutron changes into a proton, so the atomic number rises by one): $^{29}_{14}\text{Si}\rightarrow{}^{29}_{15}\text{P}+{}^{0}_{-1}e+\bar\nu$.

The two steps can be combined: $^{28}_{14}\text{Si}+{}^{1}_{0}n\rightarrow{}^{29}_{14}\text{Si}\rightarrow{}^{29}_{15}\text{P}+{}^{0}_{-1}e+\bar\nu$. (Note: in reality Si-29 is stable; the actual doping process captures a neutron in Si-30, giving Si-31, which beta-decays to P-31. The question's premise is followed here.)

questions.question: A square coil of wire of 10 turns and area $1.6\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$ passes at a constant speed into, through and out of a magnetic field of $2.0\times10^{-2}$ T (directed into the page), through positions A to E. The distance between adjacent coil positions equals the length of a coil side, and the coil takes 0.40 s to go from position A to position B. Calculate the emf induced in the coil as it enters the field.
questions.answer: The side length is $\sqrt{1.6\times10^{-3}}=0.040$ m. From A to B the coil moves a gap (0.040 m) plus one coil length (0.040 m) $=0.080$ m in 0.40 s, so $v=0.20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. It takes $\Delta t=\dfrac{0.040}{0.20}=0.20$ s to enter the field fully. $\varepsilon=N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=10\times\dfrac{(2.0\times10^{-2})(1.6\times10^{-3})}{0.20}=1.6\times10^{-3}\ \text{V}$.

questions.question: A square coil passes at constant speed into, through and out of a region of uniform magnetic field (into the page), through five positions: A (outside the field), B (entering), C (totally inside), D (exiting) and E (outside), as shown. Sketch a graph of the induced emf against position through A to E. Do not include values on the axes.
questions.answer: The emf is zero at A, C and E because the flux through the coil is not changing (no flux, or constant flux). At B the flux is increasing at a constant rate, so there is a constant emf, and at D the flux is decreasing at the same rate, so there is a constant emf of the same magnitude but opposite direction (Lenz's law). Taking the emf at B as negative: negative constant at B, positive constant at D, and zero elsewhere (the opposite sign convention is equally valid provided B and D have opposite signs).

questions.question:
Students set up a current balance. A conducting rod, 60 cm of which is within the magnetic field of two magnets, is perpendicular to the field. As the current is steadily increased, the balance reading changes because of the force on the rod. The force (calculated as $F=mg$ with $g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$) is shown in the table.

| Current (A) | Mass reading (kg) | Force (N) |
|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | $-0.55\times10^{-3}$ | $5.39\times10^{-3}$ |
| 2.1 | $-1.02\times10^{-3}$ | $9.996\times10^{-3}$ |
| 2.9 | $-1.43\times10^{-3}$ | $1.401\times10^{-2}$ |
| 3.6 | $-1.86\times10^{-3}$ | $1.823\times10^{-2}$ |
| 4.3 | $-2.15\times10^{-3}$ | $2.107\times10^{-2}$ |

Plot a graph of force versus current. Include a line of best fit.
questions.answer:
Plot current (A) on the horizontal axis and force (N, or mN) on the vertical axis, with labelled axes and units and a sensible scale. Plot the five points and draw a straight line of best fit (passing close to the origin, through or near all the points), as shown.

Note: the school's table gave forces about 100 times too small ($5.61\times10^{-5}$ N for the first reading), because the mass readings had been divided by $g$ instead of multiplied. The forces here are corrected, so the field strength in (c) differs from the school's answer ($8.3\times10^{-5}$ T).

questions.question:
Students set up a current balance. A conducting rod, 60 cm of which is within the magnetic field of two magnets, is perpendicular to the field. As the current is steadily increased, the balance reading changes because of the force on the rod. The force (calculated as $F=mg$ with $g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$) is shown in the table.

| Current (A) | Mass reading (kg) | Force (N) |
|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | $-0.55\times10^{-3}$ | $5.39\times10^{-3}$ |
| 2.1 | $-1.02\times10^{-3}$ | $9.996\times10^{-3}$ |
| 2.9 | $-1.43\times10^{-3}$ | $1.401\times10^{-2}$ |
| 3.6 | $-1.86\times10^{-3}$ | $1.823\times10^{-2}$ |
| 4.3 | $-2.15\times10^{-3}$ | $2.107\times10^{-2}$ |

Identify the relationship between force and current shown in a graph of force against current, and state TWO assumptions that must be made for this relationship to exist.
questions.answer: The graph is a straight line through the origin, so force is directly proportional to current ($F\propto I$), as $F=lIB\sin\theta$. Assumptions: the magnetic field strength $B$ is constant (uniform), the length $l$ of rod in the field is constant, and the current stays perpendicular to the field ($\theta=90^\circ$) (any two).

questions.question:
Students set up a current balance. A conducting rod, 60 cm of which is within the magnetic field of two magnets, is perpendicular to the field. As the current is steadily increased, the balance reading changes because of the force on the rod. The force (calculated as $F=mg$ with $g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$) is shown in the table.

| Current (A) | Mass reading (kg) | Force (N) |
|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | $-0.55\times10^{-3}$ | $5.39\times10^{-3}$ |
| 2.1 | $-1.02\times10^{-3}$ | $9.996\times10^{-3}$ |
| 2.9 | $-1.43\times10^{-3}$ | $1.401\times10^{-2}$ |
| 3.6 | $-1.86\times10^{-3}$ | $1.823\times10^{-2}$ |
| 4.3 | $-2.15\times10^{-3}$ | $2.107\times10^{-2}$ |

Calculate the gradient of a line of best fit of force against current and use it to determine the strength of the magnetic field. In your response, include any relevant equations.
questions.answer:
$F=lIB\sin\theta$ with $\theta=90^\circ$, so $\dfrac FI=lB$: the gradient equals $lB$. Taking two points on the line, e.g. $(2.0,\ 9.9\times10^{-3})$ and $(4.0,\ 1.97\times10^{-2})$: gradient $=\dfrac{1.97\times10^{-2}-9.9\times10^{-3}}{4.0-2.0}\approx4.9\times10^{-3}\ \text{N A}^{-1}$. Then $B=\dfrac{\text{gradient}}{l}=\dfrac{4.9\times10^{-3}}{0.60}\approx8.2\times10^{-3}$ T (accept about $8\times10^{-3}$ T).

Note: the school's table gave forces about 100 times too small ($5.61\times10^{-5}$ N for the first reading), because the mass readings had been divided by $g$ instead of multiplied. The forces here are corrected, so the field strength in (c) differs from the school's answer ($8.3\times10^{-5}$ T).

questions.question: The Standard Model identifies bosons as responsible for all the force interactions we observe. Outline the role of bosons in our universe.
questions.answer:
Bosons are the force-carrying (gauge) particles of the Standard Model, with integer spin. Matter particles (quarks and leptons) interact by exchanging bosons, which transfer energy and momentum between them.

Each fundamental force has its own boson: the strong force is carried by gluons (binding quarks into hadrons and holding nuclei together); the electromagnetic force is carried by photons (acting between charged particles); and the weak force is carried by the W and Z bosons (responsible for processes such as beta decay). Gravity is predicted to be carried by a graviton, which has not yet been detected. The Higgs boson is a different kind of boson, associated with the Higgs field that gives particles their mass.

questions.question: Students performed an investigation of the photoelectric effect using a zinc cathode. The graph of stopping voltage against frequency was extrapolated to the $y$-axis, where the line of best fit intersects at $-3.74$ V. Calculate the threshold frequency of the zinc cathode.
questions.answer: At the threshold frequency $K_{\max}=hf_0-\phi=0$, so $f_0=\dfrac\phi h$. The work function is $\phi=3.74\ \text{eV}=(3.74)(1.602\times10^{-19})=5.99\times10^{-19}$ J, so $f_0=\dfrac{5.99\times10^{-19}}{6.626\times10^{-34}}=9.04\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$.

questions.question: Students plotted stopping voltage against frequency for a zinc cathode, with the line of best fit intersecting the $y$-axis at $-3.74$ V. The investigation is repeated with a different metal with a greater work function. Describe, with a sketch, how the line of best fit will differ.
questions.answer: $eV_s=K_{\max}=hf-\phi$, so the gradient is $\dfrac he$ (the same for any metal) and the $y$-intercept is $-\dfrac\phi e$. A greater work function gives a line that is parallel to the original and below it, with a more negative $y$-intercept and a greater $x$-intercept (threshold frequency), as shown.

questions.question: In a photoelectric effect investigation, the students noticed that the photoelectrons did not all have the same velocities despite all receiving the same frequency of incident light. Account for this observation.
questions.answer: Light of a single frequency consists of photons that all have the same energy $E=hf$, and each photon transfers all of its energy to one electron. The electron then needs a different amount of energy to escape depending on where it came from: electrons in higher energy levels (and nearer the surface) need only the work function $\phi$, so they leave with the maximum kinetic energy $K_{\max}=hf-\phi$, while electrons in lower energy levels, or deeper in the metal, need more energy to escape or lose energy in collisions on the way to the surface. Their kinetic energy is the energy remaining after this, so it is smaller. Hence the electrons are emitted with a range of kinetic energies and velocities, up to a maximum.

questions.question: A pair of detectors is set up to measure the intensity of a parallel beam of unstable particles. In the reference frame of the laboratory, the detectors are separated by a distance of 45 m and the speed of the particles in the beam is $0.97c$. The intensity of the beam at the second detector is 12.5% of the intensity at the first detector. Calculate the half-life of the particles in the reference frame in which they are at rest.
questions.answer: In the particles' rest frame the detector separation is length-contracted: $l=45\sqrt{1-0.97^2}=10.9$ m. The time between detectors is $t_0=\dfrac{10.9}{0.97c}=3.8\times10^{-8}$ s. An intensity of 12.5% $=\left(\tfrac12\right)^3$ means three half-lives have elapsed, so $t_{1/2}=\dfrac{3.8\times10^{-8}}{3}=1.3\times10^{-8}\ \text{s}$ (13 ns). (Alternatively the lab time is $45/0.97c=1.55\times10^{-7}$ s, and dividing by $\gamma=4.11$ gives the same $t_0$.)

questions.question: In 1864, James Maxwell developed equations to describe the interaction of electric and magnetic fields and suggested that light was an electromagnetic wave. Outline why his work was challenged by physicists of his day and explain the eventual solution in Einstein's Theory of Special Relativity.
questions.answer:
Maxwell's equations described electric and magnetic fields propagating perpendicular to each other as an electromagnetic wave, with a speed fixed by constants of electromagnetism that matched the measured speed of light, so he concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave.

This was challenged because all known waves needed a medium, so physicists proposed a luminiferous aether as the medium for light, and Maxwell's predicted speed was independent of the observer, which clashed with Galilean relativity (the speed of light should vary for observers moving relative to the aether). The Michelson–Morley experiment used an interferometer to look for the change in the speed of light, and hence the fringe shift, expected as the Earth moved through the aether, and found none, so the aether was not detected.

Einstein's solution was to abandon the aether. His postulates were that the speed of light in a vacuum is an absolute constant for all observers, and that all inertial frames are equivalent (the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame). Since the speed of light is absolute, time and length must be relative to the motion of the observer, giving time dilation and length contraction.

questions.question: Describe one experimental evidence supporting Einstein's Theory of Special Relativity.
questions.answer:
Muons are produced in the upper atmosphere by cosmic rays and travel at close to the speed of light. Their half-life is so short (about 1.5 µs) that most should decay before reaching the Earth's surface, but many more are detected than classical physics predicts. This is explained by time dilation: for an observer on Earth, the muons' clocks run slow, so their half-life is longer (equivalently, in the muons' frame the distance to the surface is length-contracted).

(Alternatively, the Hafele–Keating experiment: atomic clocks flown around the world on aircraft differed from a clock on the ground by amounts consistent with relativity's predictions.)

questions.question: A student has a Blu-ray disc (slit separation 0.32 µm), a DVD (0.74 µm) and a CD (1.60 µm), the reflective coating of which is removed so each acts as a diffraction grating. The student also has two laser pointers: A, emitting 445 nm light, and B, emitting 636 nm light. Deduce the combination of disc and laser pointer that will produce the greatest possible number of interference maxima.
questions.answer: From $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$, the maximum order is $m_{\max}\le\dfrac d\lambda$ (since $\sin\theta\le1$), so the number of maxima is greatest when $\dfrac d\lambda$ is greatest: the largest slit separation and the shortest wavelength. This is the CD with laser pointer A: $\dfrac d\lambda=\dfrac{1600}{445}=3.6$, so $m=0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3$, giving 7 maxima.

questions.question: A student uses a CD (slit separation $1.60\ \mu\text{m}$) and a laser pointer B ($\lambda=636$ nm) in fixed positions. The horizontal laser beam is incident normally on the CD, and a diffraction pattern is produced vertically on a circular screen of diameter 30 cm, positioned 15 cm behind the CD. The height of the screen can be adjusted without changing its distance from the CD. Determine the greatest number of bright spots that can be observed on the screen.
questions.answer: $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$. For $m=1$: $\theta=\sin^{-1}\dfrac{636\times10^{-9}}{1.60\times10^{-6}}=23.4^\circ$, so $x_1=0.15\tan23.4^\circ=6.5$ cm from the central spot. For $m=2$: $\theta=\sin^{-1}(0.795)=52.7^\circ$, $x_2=0.15\tan52.7^\circ=19.7$ cm. ($m=3$ is not possible since $3\lambda/d>1$.) The spots are not equally spaced. The spots lie at $0,\ \pm6.5,\ \pm19.7$ cm. A 30 cm screen can span from $-6.5$ cm to $+19.7$ cm (26.2 cm), so it can show $m=-1,0,1,2$ (or $-2,\dots,1$), but the span for five spots would be $39.4$ cm $>30$ cm. The greatest number is 4.
